content: Jim Pankiw, born on August 7, 1966, is a Canadian politician and former Member of Parliament. He served two terms in the Canadian House of Commons, representing the Saskatoon—Humboldt constituency in Saskatchewan from 1997 to 2004. During his tenure, he was affiliated with the Reform Party of Canada, the Canadian Alliance, the Democratic Representative Caucus, and later served as an independent MP. Pankiw was raised in Unity, Saskatchewan, by his father, George Pankiw, after his mother passed away during his childhood. He trained as a chiropractor before entering politics. In the 1997 Canadian federal election, he was first elected to Parliament as a member of the Reform Party, narrowly defeating Dennis Gruending of the New Democratic Party by a margin of 220 votes. In 2000, Pankiw sparked controversy by writing a letter to Peter MacKinnon, the president of the University of Saskatchewan, criticizing the university's affirmative action policies. He compared supporters of these policies to members of the Ku Klux Klan. This letter led to a heated debate on the university campus between Pankiw and Saskatchewan Liberal Party cabinet minister Jack Hilson. At the time, Pankiw was a member of the Canadian Alliance, the successor to the Reform Party. During the 2000 federal election, he faced opposition from Liberal Party candidate and former MP Morris Bodnar in a campus debate. Despite this, Pankiw secured re-election with strong support from rural areas, winning by a margin of 6,360 votes. By 2001, Pankiw's relationship with the Canadian Alliance caucus, particularly its leader Stockwell Day, had become strained. He joined a group of MPs led by Chuck Strahl in calling for Day's resignation. As a result, Pankiw was suspended and eventually expelled from the Alliance caucus and party. He then joined other expelled MPs to form the Democratic Representative Caucus (DRC) and sat with them in a coalition with the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada. However, the election of Stephen Harper as leader of the Alliance led to the dissolution of the PC-DRC coalition, with most DRC members returning to the Alliance. Pankiw applied for re-admission but was denied due to his involvement in another controversy. An Indigenous lawyer alleged that Pankiw, while intoxicated, made lewd gestures and challenged him to a fight in a Saskatoon bar. Pankiw was also denied membership in the newly formed Conservative Party of Canada and served the remainder of his term as an independent MP. In 2003, Pankiw ran for mayor of Saskatoon against the unpopular incumbent James Maddin. Opponents of Pankiw erected billboards reading Racism-Free Zone — No Pankiw, Thank You. In response, Pankiw distributed flyers accusing his opponents of being the true racists. Criticism also arose when it was revealed that Pankiw had recently purchased a home outside Saskatoon's city limits, despite his mayoral application stating he resided in the Forest Grove area of northeast Saskatoon. Pankiw finished third in the mayoral race, ahead of Maddin but behind runner-up Peter Zakreski. Don Atchison was elected mayor, with voter turnout exceeding 50%, an unusually high level for a Canadian municipal election. Pankiw sought re-election in the 2004 federal election, running against Conservative candidate Brad Trost, Liberal Patrick Wolfe, and New Democrat Nettie Wiebe. He received 7,076 votes, finishing in fourth place, 2,368 votes behind the winner, Trost. Pankiw ran again in the 2006 federal election in the Battlefords—Lloydminster constituency but was defeated by Conservative Gerry Ritz. Ritz had represented the constituency since the 1997 election, where he defeated Pankiw's father, George, in a contentious race for the Reform Party nomination.
